title: The Last Set
subtitle: Monday and Tuesday: Forty Dollars, a Name in a Barbershop Window, a Prisoner Nobody Booked

setting.name: Kansas City, Monday 26 and Tuesday 27 October 1936
setting.description: The first two days of the calendar, nearly all of them on and around Eighteenth Street. The party works out of Matthias Hartsell's one-room office over Dandridge's Barber Shop, which is also the polling place of Precinct 14, with the voter register pasted in the window. The case begins as a missing person: a bandleader who walked out of the Gold Leaf Club at ten past four on Sunday morning and did not get home. It should end, by Tuesday night, as something much bigger: the party should know that Jules Ransom is alive in police custody under a false name and is being moved; that he took something from a white man in a camel coat who works at the Election Board; and that Jules's dead mother is registered to vote at an empty lot, along with a great many other dead people. They will not yet know what the book is, exactly, or where it is.
setting.atmosphere: A bright cold Monday with wind in the leaves and the sound trucks going up and down the Paseo. Barbershop talk: the election, the Series, whose band is leaving for New York. The Gold Leaf by day, chairs on the tables and a woman mopping, the bandstand empty, the piano closed. The Gold Leaf by night, the band playing without its leader, a little ragged and very loud, as if volume could bring him back. A station house at midnight: green paint, a radiator, a desk sergeant eating chili, and somewhere below, a man coughing. Keep these two days talkative and tense. The only fight the scenario expects is in the alley behind the Lincoln Arms, and the party can avoid it.

keyLocations.name: Dandridge's Barber Shop and the Office Upstairs
keyLocations.description: Three chairs, a shoeshine stand, a radio, a coal stove and Mr. Lucius Dandridge, sixty-one, who has cut hair on Eighteenth Street since 1909 and lets the city use his shop as the Precinct 14 polling place every election for eight dollars and the privilege. Up a narrow flight of stairs is Matthias Hartsell's office: a desk, two chairs, a filing cabinet, a corkboard, a window onto Eighteenth Street and the Gold Leaf's sign opposite.
features: In the shop window, pasted to the glass under the striped pole: OFFICIAL REGISTER OF QUALIFIED VOTERS, PRECINCT 14, SECOND WARD, Board of Election Commissioners, Kansas City, Missouri, two long sheets in small type, names and addresses
The corkboard in the office: the GM should encourage the players to use it as the case board
The office window: a clear view of the Gold Leaf's front door, and of the green Ford parked opposite it
The barbershop's telephone, a nickel a call, with Mr. Dandridge listening while he strops a razor
encounters: Geneva Hollins, the band's singer, the client
Mr. Lucius Dandridge, barber, who knows every head on Eighteenth Street and most of what is in them
Two white plainclothesmen in the green Ford, Gleason's men on loan to Lt. Voyles, watching the club
secrets: CLUE C1 (core, automatic for anyone who reads the register looking for anything to do with the Ransoms): 'Ransom, Lavinia M., 1712 Woodland Ave.' Lavinia Ransom, Jules's mother, died in February 1935. Anyone from the neighbourhood (Mr. Dandridge, Geneva, Lem Castle, Cleve Marchbanks, Dr. Mayhew) knows that 1712 Woodland burned in 1931 and is a weed lot with a chimney standing in it. Investigation DC 12, reading the whole register: at least twenty other names belong to people Mr. Dandridge knows are dead, and nineteen voters are registered at Mount Gilead Baptist Church, which nobody lives in.

Mr. Dandridge: Jules stood in front of that window for a long time in September, 'reading it like a hymn board', and went across the street to the Vine Street Democratic Club with his hat in his hand and came back without his temper. 'Whatever Horace Quarterman told him, it wasn't what he went in for.'

The green Ford: two white men, hats, cigarettes. They watch the club and anybody who goes in. Insight DC 12: they are bored and they are waiting for someone in particular. If confronted, they say they are 'from the department' and show nothing. A plate check through Lem Castle (Streetwise or simply asking a friend at the motor vehicle desk, $2) gives a car registered to the Burnham Hotel, Fifth Street. They are Harvey Gleason's men, lent to Voyles.

keyLocations.name: The Gold Leaf Club
keyLocations.description: On Eighteenth Street a few doors west of Vine: a gold-leaf sign of a trumpet, a long room under a pressed-tin ceiling, a bandstand at the back with a battered Steinway upright, a bar of dark wood, a kitchen that serves chicken and short ribs until five, a coat check by the door and a back room with a card table and a door onto the alley. The club holds two hundred. On Saturdays there are six tables by the bandstand for white customers, which Willa Templeton hates, keeps because the police and the machine prefer it, and charges double for.
features: The coat check: a half-door, a brass rail of hangers, numbered brass tags, and the kitchen door three steps away

The bandstand: the piano, ten chairs, ten music stands, the band's book (its library of arrangements) in battered folders, and Lucky Bowden's drum kit, though not its trunk, which is at the union hall
The band room behind the stand: a mirror, a sofa with the springs gone, a hot plate, a calendar from a funeral home
The alley door, and in the alley, the spot where Jules parks his green-and-cream 1934 Terraplane, which is not there
encounters: Mrs. Willa Templeton, 52, owner, sharp, tired and frightened for her licence
Zora Lattimore, 19, coat-check girl, Horace Quarterman's niece, who saves every tip for nursing school
Leander 'Lucky' Bowden, the drummer, and the rest of the band at their noon rehearsal without a leader
Pete Greenlee, 15, the band boy, who sets up the stands and carries the trunks
Tadpole, about twelve, a shoeshine boy who sleeps in the club's doorway when his aunt locks him out
secrets: CLUE B2 (core, given if Zora is approached kindly, privately, and away from her uncle's people; Persuasion or Insight DC 13, or automatic if Geneva or Dr. Mayhew is with the party): a white man in a camel overcoat, a Saturday regular at the bandstand tables, came to the coat check at ten to four 'white as a sheet' and said a book had been taken out of his coat pocket, a black book about so big. He made her turn out her bag. Then two detectives came at half past four and kept her in the back room for an hour asking who had been near the rail. 'I said nobody but the band. I didn't mean anything by it.' She will not, here, say what happened next (that is clue G1, in bn-scenario-002).

CLUE A1 (core, automatic if anyone asks Tadpole, who will tell it for a dime and a doughnut, or if Cleve Marchbanks is played): at ten past four on Sunday Jules came out of the front with his hat on and his music case, said goodnight to Tadpole and gave him a nickel, and walked round toward the alley; two white men got out of a green Ford, one showed him something in his hand that shone, and they put him in the back seat 'polite, like church ushers' and drove west. Tadpole saw the shine and says 'a badge, mister, I ain't simple'.

CLUE D1 (core, but only if someone asks Geneva or Lucky about the last few minutes before Jules left): at five past four, packing up, Jules handed Lucky a shirt rolled into a bundle and said 'Hold my laundry, Lucky, I'll get it Thursday.' Lucky put it in the bass-drum trunk with the hardware and thought no more about it. Neither of them knows what it was. The party may not realise this matters until bn-scenario-002; note it on the case board.

Willa Templeton argued loudly with Jules on Saturday because she had agreed to have the band play a machine rally at Paseo Hall on Sunday 1 November and Jules refused. She was at Varnum Bonding on Monday morning, every Monday morning, with an envelope: $40 a week for the licence. She is a red herring and a decent woman, and if the party clears her suspicion politely, she gives them the club's back room as a place to meet, and a telephone.

keyLocations.name: The Lincoln Arms Hotel
keyLocations.description: A four-storey brick hotel on Eighteenth Street for Black travellers, musicians and long-term residents, because no downtown hotel will take them: a lobby with palms and a radio, a dining room, a desk clerk named Mr. Garfield Oates who has worked nights for twenty years. Jules Ransom keeps two rooms on the third floor, 3C and 3D, with an old upright piano he bought from a church.
features: Jules's rooms, torn apart: mattress slit, drawers out, the piano's front panel off, a cabinet of piano rolls and sheet music emptied onto the floor, every book shaken and dropped
On the dresser, a photograph of a handsome woman in a church hat: Lavinia Ransom, and pinned to its frame, a funeral card, February 1935
A stack of the band's arrangements in Jules's own hand, in pencil, with titles like 'Paseo Shuffle' and 'Woodland Avenue'
The back stairs and the alley behind the hotel, where Gleason's men wait on Monday night
encounters: Mr. Garfield Oates, night desk clerk, ashamed of himself
Two Street Toughs from the Burnham Hotel, watching the back stairs on Monday night in case the book's new owner comes for Jules's things
secrets: CLUE B1 (core, automatic for anyone who looks at the rooms): this is a professional search, not a burglary. Nothing of value is gone: Jules's good watch, his cufflinks and forty dollars in a sock are still there. They were looking for something flat and the size of a book. Mr. Oates, if asked kindly or paid $5 (the same amount he was paid to forget), says two white men came at two on Sunday afternoon, showed a police card, and spent an hour up there. One wore a grey hat and had a gold tooth (Lt. Voyles's partner, Det. Sgt. Emil Kreutz).

CLUE C3 (core, for anyone who looks through Jules's music, which the searchers threw on the floor without reading): inside the pencil manuscript titled 'Woodland Avenue', between the piano part and the bass part, a folded sheet of hotel paper in Jules's handwriting: thirty-one names copied from the Precinct 14 register, each with an address and, in a second column, a date of death and the words 'M. Gilead' or 'Wheatley'. The first is his mother. At the bottom: 'Asked H.Q. 9/22. He says leave it. He says ask Strode at the Board. Strode keeps the book.' (Research or Investigation DC 12 to see that every date of death is between 1928 and 1936.)

If the party plays the 'Woodland Avenue' manuscript, it is a slow, beautiful, angry blues; Performance DC 10 to read it well enough, and anyone who hears it understands it is about his mother. No clue, but Geneva will cry, and then tell the party everything she knows.

keyLocations.name: Wheatley-Provident Hospital and Mount Gilead Baptist
keyLocations.description: Wheatley-Provident, a few blocks from Vine, is the private hospital Black physicians and nurses built in this city because the city's own hospitals would not train them and would not treat their patients with dignity; it is clean, overcrowded and always short of money. Dr. Henrietta Mayhew practises there. Mount Gilead Baptist, on Woodland, is a red-brick church with a tall white steeple whose pastor, the Rev. Zebulon Pettus, has buried most of the neighbourhood's dead for nineteen years and keeps every burial in a leather book.
features: The hospital records room in the basement, where every death certificate the hospital's doctors sign is copied in a bound register
The church office: Rev. Pettus's burial book, a coal stove, a framed photograph of the 1927 choir
Mount Gilead's own address on the Precinct 14 register, as the residence of nineteen voters
encounters: Mrs. Inez Purvis, the hospital's records nurse, who will help a doctor and nobody else
Rev. Zebulon Pettus, 64, a big slow man with a voice like an organ, who is a Republican and has been for sixty-four years
secrets: CLUE C2 (core, automatic for Dr. Mayhew, or for anyone she sends, or for anyone who persuades Mrs. Purvis, Persuasion DC 14): the hospital register for 12 February 1935: Ransom, Lavinia Mae, 61, lobar pneumonia, H. Mayhew M.D. Dr. Mayhew signed it. She remembers the night.

Rev. Pettus, shown the register or Jules's list: he buried every one of the nineteen people registered at his church. 'They are on the rolls of the Lord, sir. I did not know they were on the rolls of the Board of Election Commissioners.' His burial book corroborates every date on Jules's list (C3). He will, if asked, take the party through the rest of the precinct in bn-scenario-002.

Dr. Mayhew, or anyone checking the hospital's own outgoing paperwork (Research DC 13): the city's Health Department receives a copy of every certificate. A clerk from the Health Department came to the hospital in June to 'reconcile the colored files' and took away a list. His name was Fry.

keyLocations.name: Number Four District Station and the Impound Lot
keyLocations.description: The police station that covers Eighteenth Street: a soot-brown brick building with a green lamp over the door, a front desk behind a brass rail, a squad room, and in the basement, eight cells. Its commander and all its sergeants are white; four of its forty patrolmen are Black, and Lem Castle is one. The impound lot is behind it, a cinder yard with a chain-link fence.
features: The front desk, the blotter and the booking cards in a wooden file, and Sergeant Dennis Mulvane eating chili
The basement cells, reached by an iron stair, and the trusties, two Black prisoners serving thirty days, who carry the meals down from the kitchen and count the plates
The impound lot: twenty cars, and among them a green-and-cream 1934 Terraplane with a dent in the rear fender and the band's name painted small on the spare-tire cover
The back door to the alley, where the prisoner van loads at midnight
encounters: Sergeant Dennis Mulvane, desk sergeant, who takes ten dollars and is afraid of Lt. Voyles
Lt. Conrad Voyles, Homicide, who drops in on Monday night and introduces himself to anyone asking about Jules Ransom
Mr. Clifton Bynum, a trusty, fifty, who has been carrying plates down the iron stairs for three Octobers
secrets: CLUE A2 (core, automatic for anyone who looks into the impound lot, Lem Castle with no questions asked, anyone else for $2 to the attendant): Jules's Terraplane, towed on Sunday at 6:10 a.m. on a Number Four District tow slip with no case number, signed 'by order Lt. V.'. The car has been searched: seat cushions out, door panels pried.

CLUE A3 (core, from the trusty Clifton Bynum, to Lem Castle or to anyone who gives him a pack of cigarettes and a straight answer): one extra plate Sunday and Monday, carried to the end cell for a prisoner listed on the kitchen slip as 'John Ransome, hold for Lt. V.'. 'He's a piano player. He's hurt. He ain't said a word to them, I'll tell you that.' The front-desk blotter shows no such prisoner (A3 proves the blotter is a lie).

CLUE A4 (core, if Dr. Henrietta Mayhew is played, or if the party has asked her to stand by): at 11:20 on Monday night the station telephones Wheatley-Provident, because the city surgeon will not come out for a Black prisoner at that hour, asking for a doctor for 'a colored prisoner who fell down the stairs'. It is Jules: two broken ribs, a split eyebrow, bruising from a rubber hose across the back and thighs. He has five minutes with her, a white patrolman at the door. He tells her: 'Don't let them find out who I gave my laundry to. Tell Geneva I'm sorry about Thursday.' He will not say more with the patrolman there. Diagnosis: he is not in danger of dying this week if nobody hits him again.

At midnight on Monday the van takes Jules to Number Six District in Westport. The party, if watching the back door, sees it go. On Tuesday the trusty says the end cell is empty and the plate went back up. This is the first turn of the merry-go-round (see campaignRules).

synopsis: On Monday morning Geneva Hollins, singer with the Jules Ransom Orchestra, hires Matthias Hartsell with the band's kitty to find her bandleader, who walked out of the Gold Leaf Club at ten past four on Sunday morning and vanished. The police will not look. The party pieces together the last set: a white Saturday regular in a camel coat who lost 'a book' from his overcoat at the coat check; a coat-check girl who was questioned for an hour by detectives and is frightened of more than them; a shoeshine boy who saw two white men with a badge put Jules into a green Ford; a hotel room searched by professionals who left the money and took nothing; and, hidden in a pencil manuscript called 'Woodland Avenue', Jules's own list of thirty-one dead people registered to vote in Precinct 14, beginning with his mother, and a note that says Strode keeps the book. In the barbershop window under the party's own office, Lavinia Ransom, who died in 1935 and whose death certificate Dr. Mayhew signed, is registered at an empty lot. On Monday night Jules's Terraplane turns up in the police impound lot on an unnumbered tow slip, a trusty counts one extra plate for a prisoner the blotter does not show, and a doctor is called in at midnight to a 'colored prisoner who fell'. By then Lt. Conrad Voyles of Homicide has introduced himself, very pleasantly, and at midnight the prisoner van takes Jules somewhere else. The party ends Tuesday knowing that Jules is alive and in the hands of the police, that he took a book from a man at the Election Board, that the book is about the dead on the voter rolls, and that the police are moving him so that nobody can find him. The questions for bn-scenario-002 are where he is now, where the book is, and what is in it.
hook: Monday 26 October 1936, eleven in the morning, the office over Dandridge's Barber Shop on Eighteenth Street. The radio downstairs is playing the election, a sound truck is going by on the Paseo with a brass band on a phonograph, and Geneva Hollins has put a cigar box on the desk with forty dollars in it. 'Jules Ransom,' she says. 'Thirty-three years old, five foot ten, plays piano like the Lord's own left hand. He walked out of the Gold Leaf at ten past four Sunday morning and he never got home.'

conclusions.conclusion: A. Jules is alive, in police custody off the books, and being moved
clues: A1: Tadpole (or Cleve) saw the badge and the green Ford (the Gold Leaf)
A2: the Terraplane on an unnumbered tow slip signed 'Lt. V.' (the impound lot)
A3: the trusty's extra plate for 'John Ransome' (Number Four's cells)
A4: Dr. Mayhew treats him at midnight (Number Four)

conclusions.conclusion: B. Jules took a book from a white man in a camel coat, and the man works at the Election Board
clues: B1: the professional search of his rooms (the Lincoln Arms)
B2: Zora Lattimore and the lost book (the coat check)
B3: Beatrice Albright recognises Virgil Strode (her own memory of Saturday, or the Monitor's photograph files)
B4: Casey Dudek's errand, or a Gleason man in the alley who says it (the Lincoln Arms alley)
C3's last line: 'Strode keeps the book' (Jules's manuscript)

conclusions.conclusion: C. The dead of Eighteenth Street are registered to vote at false addresses
clues: C1: Lavinia Ransom on the register in Dandridge's window, at an empty lot
C2: Dr. Mayhew's death certificate for her (Wheatley-Provident)
C3: Jules's list of thirty-one names (the 'Woodland Avenue' manuscript)
Rev. Pettus's burial book and the nineteen voters registered at his church (Mount Gilead)

acts.title: Act 1: Forty Dollars
acts.description: Monday morning and afternoon. The client, the barbershop window, and the Gold Leaf by daylight. This act is conversation and should take about an hour of play. Let the players meet Eighteenth Street and let Eighteenth Street look the white members of the party over. By the end of it they should have the last set reconstructed, Tadpole's account, and at least the name on the register.
objectives: Hear Geneva out and take the case (or take it for less than forty dollars, which Eighteenth Street will remember)
Read the register in Dandridge's window
Reconstruct Jules's last hour at the Gold Leaf
Find out who saw him leave

scenes.name: The Cigar Box
scenes.description: Geneva's account. She is precise and controlled and has not slept. She knows: Jules played the last set, the band packed up at four, he said goodnight at ten past and went out the front because he always says goodnight to Tadpole. His car is gone. His rooms at the Lincoln Arms were torn apart on Sunday afternoon (Mr. Oates told her). Number Four District told her a musician who stays out is not a missing person. She also knows the band plays Thursday, and without Jules there is no band; she has a record date in Chicago on 12 November with the whole orchestra, the first of her life, and she will not say that out loud because it feels like selfishness. She does not know about the book. She will mention, if asked whether Jules had trouble, that he had been 'strange since September, angry the way he gets quiet', and that he and Mrs. Templeton argued on Saturday.
scenes.readAloud: She sits down without taking off her gloves, a slim woman of twenty-seven in a church hat with a small brave feather in it and a coat too thin for October, and she opens the cigar box and turns it so you can see: ones and fives, a few silver dollars, and on top a dance ticket from Paseo Hall with a figure in pencil: $40.00, Ransom Orch. Kitty. 'That's every man in the band,' she says. 'Lucky put in eight dollars and he hasn't got eight dollars.' Downstairs, through the floor, Mr. Dandridge's radio says something about the President and somebody laughs. She does not. 'They told me at the station a colored musician who stays out late isn't a missing person. I'd like to hire somebody who thinks he is.'

skillChecks.success: She is telling the truth and holding something back that is not about the case: hope, embarrassment, something with a date on it. If gently asked, she tells you about Chicago. It makes her more of a person and the deadline more real: the band needs Jules by 12 November or the date goes to someone else.
skillChecks.failure: She seems composed and businesslike; you learn the facts and not the woman. She tells you about Chicago later, in Act 2, when she has seen how hard you work.

skillChecks.success: If the party asks about the last minutes before Jules left, she remembers him handing Lucky a bundled shirt: CLUE D1. She does not think it matters.
skillChecks.failure: She does not remember anything special about the last minutes. Lucky does, if asked at the rehearsal.

scenes.name: The Register in the Window
scenes.description: Dandridge's window and Mr. Dandridge. Anyone who reads the register looking for Ransom finds Lavinia (C1). Mr. Dandridge knows she is dead; everyone on Eighteenth Street knows 1712 Woodland is a weed lot. The rest of the register rewards a long look. Mr. Dandridge also gives the September story: Jules reading the window, crossing to the Vine Street Democratic Club, coming back without his temper.
scenes.readAloud: The register is two long sheets of cheap paper pasted inside the glass, already curling at the corners, names and addresses in tiny type in three columns, and the morning sun comes through it so that the names show backwards on Mr. Dandridge's linoleum. Inside, a man is asleep in the second chair under a hot towel, and Mr. Dandridge, small, bald and immaculate in a white jacket, is stropping a razor and watching you read. 'You looking for anybody in particular?' he says. 'Because I can tell you who's alive on that list a lot faster than you can.'

skillChecks.success: Reading the whole register with Mr. Dandridge's help: at least twenty-two names belong to people he knows are dead, nineteen voters are registered at Mount Gilead Baptist, forty-four at an address that turns out to be Hargrove's coal yard, and eleven at a house that burned in 1934. Precinct 14 has 1,412 registered voters. Mr. Dandridge says there are maybe nine hundred grown people living in it, 'and half of them never registered because they've been told it isn't for them'.
skillChecks.failure: There are a lot of names. You find Lavinia Ransom and two or three others Mr. Dandridge knows are dead, and the sense that there are more.

skillChecks.success: Mr. Dandridge trusts you with his opinion: Horace Quarterman runs the Second Ward and has done for twelve years, and he is 'not a bad man, just a man who has decided what he can afford'. Quarterman's club is where the coal tickets and the city jobs come from, and if you want to know who put a dead woman on the rolls, 'you don't ask Horace, you watch who Horace is scared of'.
skillChecks.failure: Mr. Dandridge says politics is not a barbershop subject, which it always is.

scenes.name: Noon at the Gold Leaf
scenes.description: The band rehearses at noon without its leader, Geneva or Lucky at the piano. Willa Templeton watches from the bar. Zora Lattimore is folding napkins. Tadpole is outside. This scene can run long: let the players talk to the band (ten men with ten opinions about Jules, the music, the machine and New York), to Mrs. Templeton (the argument, the envelope, her licence), to Zora (B2, carefully), and to Tadpole (A1).
scenes.readAloud: In daylight the Gold Leaf is a long brown room that smells of floor soap and last night's cigarettes, the chairs up on the tables like legs in the air, and at the back, under one bulb, nine men in shirtsleeves and hats are playing a slow number in B-flat with nobody at the piano. It sounds like a house with a room missing. The drummer, a huge man with a gentle face and a boxer's ear, is playing brushes so softly you can hear the brushes. When the tune ends, nobody says anything, and then the second trumpet says 'Again,' and they play it again.

skillChecks.success: Zora Lattimore, taken aside: CLUE B2. If Dr. Mayhew or Geneva is present, no roll is needed.
skillChecks.failure: Zora says she saw nothing and goes to the kitchen. She is watching the party, and she will come to Matthias's office on Tuesday night by herself if they were kind to her.

skillChecks.success: The band's talk: the rumour on the street this morning is that Jules owed a numbers banker four hundred dollars and ran. Every man in the band says it is a lie. The trombonist says he heard it first at the Vine Street Democratic Club at nine this morning, 'from Horace's own doorman'. CLUE G3: a rumour planted by Quarterman.
skillChecks.failure: You hear the numbers rumour and that the band does not believe it.

skillChecks.success: Mrs. Templeton is frightened, not guilty. If you say so to her, kindly, she tells you about the envelope to Varnum Bonding every Monday, the machine rally Jules refused to play, and that she would sell the club before she gave up a musician to the police. She offers the back room and the telephone.
skillChecks.failure: Mrs. Templeton is guarded and short and makes it clear that white customers (if any of the party are white) are welcome on Saturdays at the bandstand tables, at double price. She is testing you.

encounters: No fights expected. The green Ford's two men (Street Tough) will step out to look anyone over who goes into the Gold Leaf more than once; they do nothing else in daylight

acts.title: Act 2: Where He Isn't
acts.description: Monday afternoon and night. The Lincoln Arms and the rooms (B1, C3), the hospital and the church (C2), the Gold Leaf at night with the band playing for its life, and Beatrice Albright's Saturday memory (B3). If the party lingers at the hotel after dark, the two Burnham men in the alley (B4). At 11:20 the telephone call to Wheatley-Provident (A4), if a doctor is in the party or on call.
objectives: Search Jules's rooms and find what the searchers missed
Confirm that Lavinia Ransom is dead and where she is registered
Identify the man in the camel coat
Survive, or avoid, the alley behind the Lincoln Arms

scenes.name: Rooms 3C and 3D
scenes.description: The searched rooms. B1 is automatic. C3 is automatic for anyone who looks through the music, which the searchers threw on the floor. Mr. Oates at the desk can give the two men's descriptions for kindness or five dollars. The rooms tell the party about Jules: a tidy man, a reader, a church piano, a photograph of his mother, a drawer of letters from musicians in New York, a savings book with $612 in it at the Peoples Finance bank, which a man who owes the numbers four hundred would not have.
scenes.readAloud: The door to 3C has been opened with a shoulder and closed again with care, which tells you something. Inside, someone has taken the room apart the way a mechanic takes apart an engine: the mattress slit end to end and the stuffing pulled out in neat handfuls, every drawer out and turned over on the bed, the front panel of an old church upright leaning against the wall so that you can see its hammers, like teeth. Sheet music is everywhere, hundreds of pages in pencil and ink, trodden on. On the dresser, untouched, is a gold watch and a photograph of a woman in a church hat who has Jules Ransom's eyes, and tucked into the corner of the frame, a funeral card.

skillChecks.success: The search went in an order: bed, drawers, piano, music cabinet, the backs of pictures, the toilet tank. Professionals who knew what size the thing was. Whatever they wanted is the size of a book, and they did not find it (they would not have kept going into the toilet tank if they had).
skillChecks.failure: It is a mess; you learn they did not take the money or the watch, which is B1.

skillChecks.success: Reading or playing 'Woodland Avenue' on the gutted upright (it still plays, out of tune): it is a blues about a woman, a house and a fire, and anyone from Eighteenth Street who hears it knows it is Lavinia. Geneva, if present, tells the party everything she knows and some things she had decided not to say: that Jules went to see Horace Quarterman in September and came back 'with a face like a shut door'.
skillChecks.failure: It is a pencil manuscript; it is beautiful even on paper. The list inside it (C3) is found either way.

skillChecks.success: Comparing the thirty-one names: every death is between 1928 and 1936, every one at Mount Gilead or Wheatley-Provident, and every address is one Jules has written a small cross beside, which on the register means 'Dandridge knows it is not a house'.
skillChecks.failure: It is a list of dead people and their churches. The pattern can wait for Rev. Pettus.

scenes.name: The Man in the Camel Coat
scenes.description: Beatrice Albright was at the Gold Leaf on Saturday night with a party from the Country Club District, slumming, and is ashamed of it. She saw the man in the camel coat at the next table, because he was the only one there who listened to the music instead of talking over it, and she knows his face: Virgil Strode, deputy chief clerk of the Board of Election Commissioners, whose photograph the Monitor ran in August above a story about the new registration machines. If Beatrice is not played, any reporter or the Monitor's photo morgue can identify Strode from Zora's description (Research DC 13), or Willa Templeton knows him by sight and as 'Mr. S., tips a dollar, likes the ballads'.
scenes.readAloud: He was at the next table on Saturday, alone, which was why you noticed him: a narrow, balding man in a good camel-hair coat he did not take off until the second set, drinking ginger ale. Everyone at your table was talking, laughing too loudly, being seen, and he was listening. When the band played a ballad he closed his eyes. When the piano player took a chorus by himself, the man in the camel coat put down his glass and did not pick it up again until it was over. You had thought, at the time, that he was the only person in the room who had paid for the right thing.

skillChecks.success: The Monitor's photograph files: Virgil Strode, deputy chief clerk, Board of Election Commissioners, with a new registration machine, August 1936; also a 1934 photograph of him standing behind Big Sid Varnum at a Democratic dinner at the Muehlebach. He is a widower, lives at the Hotel Savoy, and has run registration for the east side wards since 1930. CLUE B3 confirmed.
skillChecks.failure: You know the face and not yet the name. The Monitor's files have it in an hour on Tuesday.

skillChecks.success: Beatrice's own world: her father, the bond lawyer Prescott Albright, does Varnum Bonding's legal work. Strode has been to dinner at the house on Ward Parkway. Her father calls him 'Sid's bookkeeper' and does not like him, 'which in Father means he is afraid of him'.
skillChecks.failure: You know Strode is a machine man, and nothing about him as a person.

scenes.name: The Alley Behind the Lincoln Arms
scenes.description: If the party leaves the Lincoln Arms by the back after dark on Monday, or carries anything out of Jules's rooms, two Burnham men (Street Tough) step out of the alley with a bat and a sap and ask for 'the book the piano player took'. They have been told it might be in his rooms and that whoever comes for his things knows where it is. They are not trying to kill anyone. They say B4 out loud. If Casey Dudek is played, he knows one of them, Sonny Moss, from the Burnham, and can end it with a word, at the price of being seen with the party.
scenes.readAloud: The alley is brick on both sides and smells of coal smoke and garbage, and the only light is a bulb in a cage over the hotel kitchen door. Two men step out of a doorway, white men in caps and work jackets, one with a baseball bat held low along his leg the way a man holds something he is not proud of. 'Evening,' says the one without the bat. 'We're looking for a book the piano player took off a gentleman. Black book. About so big. You give us that and we'll all go home.'

skillChecks.success: They back off. One of them, going, says 'Gleason's going to want to know who you are'. Heat +1.
skillChecks.failure: They try their luck. A short, ugly fight (two Street Toughs); they run when one goes down. Heat +1 if anyone shoots.

skillChecks.success: You convince them the book was already taken by the police on Sunday. They go away happy and tell Gleason, who tells Strode, who gets one more day of hope and stops watching the hotel.
skillChecks.failure: They do not believe you, but they are not paid enough to fight about it. They leave, and they will recognise you.

encounters: Two Street Toughs from the Burnham Hotel in the Lincoln Arms alley (optional; they run when one goes down)
The green Ford's men, who follow anyone who leaves the Gold Leaf with Geneva after midnight (they want to know where she sleeps)

acts.title: Act 3: The Station House
acts.description: Monday night to Tuesday night. Number Four District, its impound lot, its trusties and its desk sergeant. Lt. Conrad Voyles drops in and is charming. At 11:20 on Monday the call for a doctor (A4). At midnight the van to Westport. On Tuesday the party confirms the move, finds the car, and may visit the Vine Street Democratic Club, where Horace Quarterman will not discuss Jules at all, kindly. At the end of Tuesday, Zora Lattimore comes to Matthias's office alone.
objectives: Prove that Jules is in police custody
Get a message to him or from him
Meet Lt. Voyles without making an enemy too soon
Learn that he has been moved and work out what that means

scenes.name: Sergeant Mulvane's Desk
scenes.description: The front desk at Number Four. Sergeant Mulvane says there is no Julius Ransom in his cells, which is true by the blotter. For ten dollars he will look at the booking cards, which do not show him either. Lem Castle can go downstairs; anyone else needs a reason, a bribe or the trusties. Clifton Bynum, carrying plates, gives A3 to Lem or to anyone who gives him cigarettes and a straight answer. The impound lot gives A2. Lt. Voyles comes in at about ten on Monday night, hears there are people asking about Ransom, and introduces himself: courteous, soft-spoken, a big pale man with small soft hands and rimless glasses, who says the department is very concerned and will let them know if anything turns up.
scenes.readAloud: The station house is green paint, brown linoleum, a brass rail worn bright by elbows and a radiator that clanks like a man hitting it with a wrench. Behind the desk a red-faced sergeant is eating chili from a paper carton with a wooden spoon, reading the racing page. Behind him is a wall of pigeonholes, a calendar from a coal company and a door with a wired-glass window, and through the floor, faintly, you can hear someone coughing, the long hard cough of a man with something broken inside him.

skillChecks.success: Talking to Voyles: he already knows every name in the party. He asks, gently, whether Jules ever gave anybody anything to hold. He is not looking for Jules. He is looking for something Jules had. Heat +1 just for being memorable to him.
skillChecks.failure: Voyles seems like a decent, worried senior officer. That is what he is for.

skillChecks.success: Clifton Bynum, or any Black patrolman at Number Four, explains the merry-go-round: hold a man 'for investigation', keep him off the blotter, move him every day or two under a different misspelling, and a writ never catches up. 'They do it to our people every week. They just don't usually do it to somebody anybody's looking for.'
skillChecks.failure: The trusty says only that the end cell is a 'hold for the lieutenant' and that those don't stay long.

scenes.name: A Colored Prisoner Who Fell
scenes.description: At 11:20 on Monday the station telephones Wheatley-Provident for a doctor, because the city surgeon will not come out at that hour for a Black prisoner. If Dr. Mayhew is played she takes the call (or is woken by it). If not, and the party has made friends at the hospital, a nurse telephones Matthias's office: 'They've sent for Dr. Mayhew at Number Four, and Dr. Mayhew says you'll want to know.' Five minutes with Jules (A4), a white patrolman at the door, and the message about his laundry and Thursday. Then at midnight the van leaves by the back door for Westport.
scenes.readAloud: The end cell is six feet by eight, a cot, a bucket, a bulb in a wire cage, and the man on the cot tries to stand up when the door opens and cannot. He is slim and dark and handsome under the damage, with a split eyebrow crusted black and his right arm held tight against his ribs, and he is still wearing the trousers of a good dinner suit and one patent shoe. When he sees who has come he laughs, very carefully, because laughing hurts. 'Well,' he says. 'Somebody's looking.'

skillChecks.success: You bind his ribs and clean the eye. He can breathe properly for the first time since Sunday, and he trusts you. He says, under the patrolman's hearing: 'Don't let them find out who I gave my laundry to. Tell Geneva I'm sorry about Thursday.' And: 'Strode's book. My mother's in it. All of them are.'
skillChecks.failure: You patch him well enough. He says only the line about laundry and Thursday before the patrolman says time.

skillChecks.success: You pass him something (a pencil stub and a cigarette paper, a nickel, a note from Geneva) without the patrolman seeing. He will use the pencil: this is how D2 gets out of Number Six in bn-scenario-002.
skillChecks.failure: The patrolman sees and takes it, and reports it, and Voyles is a little more interested in the party. Heat +1.

scenes.name: Horace Quarterman's Club
scenes.description: On Tuesday the party may go to the Vine Street Democratic Club, over a furniture store on Vine: a long room with a portrait of the President, a coal-ticket window, three telephones, a dozen men waiting on benches for jobs, bail and favours, and at the end a glassed-in office with Horace Quarterman in it. He is fifty-eight, heavy, beautifully dressed, warm, and tired to the bone. He will not discuss Jules except to say he is 'making inquiries through the proper channels' and that the party should not stir up the police, for everybody's sake, and especially for Jules's. He will discuss the vote, the machine, the coal and the jobs at length and with conviction. He does not know yet how much the party knows. Do not let him give anything away here except his fear. Insight DC 15: when Jules's name is said, he looks at the telephone on his desk.
scenes.readAloud: The man in the glass office stands up when you come in, which is the first thing you notice, and comes round the desk to shake hands, which is the second. He is big and grey and dressed better than anybody you have seen this week, a pearl stickpin, a watch chain, a carnation, and his hand is warm and dry. Behind him on the wall is the President, a calendar from the Board of Public Works, and a framed photograph of a girl in a white Lincoln High School graduation dress. 'Sit down,' he says. 'Everybody's worried about Jules. I'm worried about Jules. Now, let's all be careful, because worry makes people do foolish things in this town, and foolish things get people hurt.'

skillChecks.success: He is not lying about being worried. He is lying about something else, and it is personal: his eyes went to the girl in the photograph when the police were mentioned. (It is Zora.)
skillChecks.failure: He is a politician; he is worried; he is not going to help. That is all you see.

skillChecks.success: He gives the party something, to buy time: 'If a man were being held, and I'm not saying he is, he'd be safest held quiet until after Tuesday. After Tuesday, everybody calms down.' It is the most honest thing he says, and it is wrong.
skillChecks.failure: He thanks you for coming and asks one of his men to see you out, and the man does, closely.

encounters: Lt. Conrad Voyles (Bent Detective) and Det. Sgt. Emil Kreutz (Crooked Cop), at Number Four on Monday night; no fight unless the party starts one in a police station, which would be Heat +3 and a cell
The green Ford, which on Tuesday night follows Zora Lattimore to Matthias's office and parks outside

npcsInvolved.name: Geneva Hollins, 27
npcsInvolved.role: The band's singer; the client; a companion (full sheet in the companion files)
npcsInvolved.description: Slim, composed, a church hat with one brave feather, a voice that fills the Gold Leaf without a microphone. Knows everybody on Eighteenth Street and what they owe each other.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Find Jules alive, keep the band together, and get to Chicago on 12 November without feeling she has traded one for the other.

npcsInvolved.name: Lt. Conrad Voyles, 51
npcsInvolved.role: Homicide lieutenant; the machine's man in the police; the main antagonist
npcsInvolved.description: Big, pale, rimless glasses, small soft hands, a deacon's voice. Never raises it. Remembers every name. Use Bent Detective.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Recover the book for Strode and Varnum, then make Jules and anyone who knows too much disappear. A captaincy has been promised.

npcsInvolved.name: Zora Lattimore, 19
npcsInvolved.role: Coat-check girl at the Gold Leaf; Horace Quarterman's niece
npcsInvolved.description: Small, quick, very proper, a nurse's-school prospectus in her handbag and $86 of saved tips in a coffee can. Frightened of the police and more frightened that she caused this.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Undo what she said on Sunday morning without getting her uncle hurt.

npcsInvolved.name: Willa Templeton, 52
npcsInvolved.role: Owner of the Gold Leaf Club
npcsInvolved.description: Tall, gold-rimmed spectacles, a ledger of her own she keeps in her head. Pays the machine forty dollars a week and despises every dollar of it.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Keep her licence, her staff and her band, in that order on bad days and the reverse on good ones.

npcsInvolved.name: Mr. Lucius Dandridge, 61
npcsInvolved.role: Barber; landlord of Matthias's office; the Precinct 14 polling place
npcsInvolved.description: Small, bald, immaculate, a white jacket and an encyclopaedic memory for who on Eighteenth Street is alive.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To see an honest count in his shop once before he dies.

npcsInvolved.name: Horace Quarterman, 58
npcsInvolved.role: Second Ward leader; the Vine Street Democratic Club
npcsInvolved.description: Big, grey, beautifully dressed, warm handshake, exhausted eyes. Twelve years of coal tickets and city jobs, and a ward that votes as he asks.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Protect Zora; get Jules through the election alive; keep the ward's jobs; and never be asked what he did on Sunday at 4 a.m.

npcsInvolved.name: Tadpole, about 12
npcsInvolved.description: Small, sharp, sleeps in the Gold Leaf doorway when his aunt locks him out. Charges a dime and a doughnut for the truth. Never put him in danger on screen; the GM should let the party protect him.
npcsInvolved.motivation: A doughnut, a dime, and for somebody to believe him.

npcsInvolved.name: Clifton Bynum, 50
npcsInvolved.role: Jail trusty at Number Four District
npcsInvolved.description: Grey, slow, a voice like gravel, serving thirty days for being drunk on a Saturday on the wrong side of Troost Avenue. Counts the plates.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Do his thirty days, and not watch another man go out of the end cell feet first.

npcsInvolved.name: Rev. Zebulon Pettus, 64
npcsInvolved.role: Pastor of Mount Gilead Baptist; keeper of the burial book
npcsInvolved.description: A big slow man with a voice like an organ, a lifelong Republican, who has buried most of the people in Precinct 14's register.
npcsInvolved.motivation: That the dead be let rest, and that the living be let vote.

rewards.money: The band's $40 retainer (paid Monday morning; Matthias's rate is $10 a day, so it buys four days, which the party may honour or stretch as they like; split as the party wishes and add each share to the wallet line). Willa Templeton adds $25 if they prove Jules is alive. Anything the party takes from the alley toughs is about $6.
items: Jules's list of thirty-one names from the 'Woodland Avenue' manuscript (Clue C3)
A copy of the hospital register entry for Lavinia Ransom (Clue C2)
The Number Four tow slip, or a note of it, signed 'by order Lt. V.' (Clue A2)
Virgil Strode's name and photograph from the Monitor files (Clue B3)
Lt. Voyles's card, with a home telephone number written on the back 'in case you hear anything'
Zora Lattimore's trust, if the party was kind to her, which on Tuesday night brings her to the office

twists: Jules is not missing. He is in the custody of the police, who are moving him so that nobody can find him. This is the first big reveal and should land by Monday midnight at the latest; it turns a missing-person case into a race.

The man who gave Jules up to the police was not Strode or Voyles but Horace Quarterman, the Black ward leader, to save his niece. Plant it now (the photograph in his office, the glance at the telephone, the numbers rumour from his club) and reveal it in bn-scenario-002. Quarterman is not a villain; he made a bargain he believed in with a man who lied to him.

Jules gave the book to Lucky Bowden in a rolled shirt, and neither Lucky nor Geneva knows what it was. The party may hear the 'laundry' line from Geneva, Lucky and Jules himself in this scenario and not understand it. That is fine; on the case board it should be written down.

The man who lost the book, Virgil Strode, is not a thug. He is a lonely, careful man who loves the music on Eighteenth Street and has spent the summer stealing the names of its dead. Let the players see the contradiction and not resolve it for them.
The two men in the green Ford are not police. They are Gleason's men from the Burnham Hotel, lent to Voyles, which is how the machine works: everyone is everyone else's.
dmTips: This scenario establishes Eighteenth Street, the client and the calendar. Budget about an hour for Act 1, ninety minutes for Act 2 and an hour for Act 3. The only expected fight is in the alley, and the party can avoid it.

Core clues are automatic. Anyone who reads the register looking for Ransom finds Lavinia (C1); anyone who looks at the searched rooms sees it was professional (B1); anyone who looks through the music finds the list (C3); anyone who sees the Terraplane sees the slip (A2). Rolls add detail, save a scene or avoid Heat.

The color line is in every scene. Let the white characters notice how differently they are treated on Eighteenth Street (politely, distantly, assumed to be police or slummers) and how differently their Black colleagues are treated at Number Four. Do it through specific people, not lectures. Sergeant Mulvane calls Lem Castle 'Castle' and Beatrice Albright 'Miss'. Let the players feel it.
Play Voyles as the most courteous man in the city. He should be likeable for five minutes. His menace is that he already knows their names.

Tadpole is a child. He gives his clue and the party should want to protect him; do not put him in harm's way on screen. If the party is careless with his name, have Mr. Dandridge take the boy in for the week.
Start the calendar visibly: put the days on the table, Monday 26 October to Tuesday 3 November, and cross off scenes. Say the time when the party arrives anywhere.
If the party has not found the list in the manuscript by Tuesday, have Geneva go to the rooms to collect Jules's music for Thursday and find it herself, or have Zora say 'Strode' in Act 3.

Music: describe it. The Gold Leaf at night with the band playing without its leader should be one of the scenes the players remember. A borrowed pianist from another band sits in, and he is good, and he is not Jules, and everybody can hear it.

Period texture: Roosevelt's speeches on every radio, sound trucks, Landon sunflowers on a few white lapels, the World Series talk in the barbershop, five-cent beer, ten-cent chili, a forty-cent cab. The new City Hall tower going up downtown, its steel frame lit at night.
Level-up note: the 1800 XP in this file is per character and takes each 3rd-level character to 4th (2,700 XP). Award it when the party learns Jules has been moved, whatever else they have found.
